title: What does the song rest on?
hookLine: three singers sit down to talk shop, and one keeps asking: what holds that up? the answer goes all the way to space
carry: the last ground of everything is brahman
tomorrow: which Veda does Krishna call himself?

cards: Why is the sky blue? Because of the light. Why?
Because of the air. Why? Small children play this at bedtime, and the questions stop only when someone runs out of answers, or patience.
The Chandogya Upanishad tells a story that runs like that. Three men skilled in the high chant of the Sama Veda sit down to talk about it, two brahmins and a king.
And one question keeps getting asked, each time one step further down: what does that rest on?

teach.b: Their names are Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. Pravahana, the king, says: you two speak first; I'll listen. So Shilaka asks Dalbhya, in paraphrase: what does the saman, the chant, rest on?
Dalbhya says: on tone, the sound of the voice. And tone? On breath.
And breath? On food. And food?
On water. And water? On that world, the heavens.
And the heavens? Here Dalbhya stops. We don't lead the chant past the heavens, he says; we set it there.
Shilaka isn't satisfied. The heavens, he says, rest on this world, the earth beneath us. Then Shilaka puts the question to the king: and this world, what does it rest on?

teach.h: AND THE EARTH? IT RESTS ON SPACE.
teach.b: All beings come out of space and go back into space, he says. Space is greater than all of them, the last support. Here the teaching opens wide.

teach.h: THE BRAHMA SUTRA: THAT SPACE IS BRAHMAN.
teach.b: The Brahma Sutra, the classic summary of the Upanishads, stops at this very passage and asks: what is this space? Its answer, followed by Vedanta's great teachers, Shankara and Ramanuja among them: not empty air.
It's Brahman, the one reality all beings come from and go back to, since only Brahman could be the source and end of everything.

That's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, arriving in a talk between three singers: under the song, the breath, the food and the earth, there is Brahman. A note only rings because there's room around it.
In this teaching, everything rings in Brahman.

how: The dialogue of Shilaka, Dalbhya and King Pravahana is taught from the Chandogya Upanishad, part of the Sama Veda's tradition, as a meditation on the high chant resting finally on space.

games.q: what does “the sama veda as song” mean?
o: a chant resting, step by step, on open space
a chant resting on the king's command alone
a chant that rests on nothing and soon fades

games.q: what the chant rests on — tap the pairs.
p: rests on space, says the king

s: the three singers agree on the answer from the start
Dalbhya stops at the heavens, Shilaka goes to the earth, and the king goes on to space.
King Pravahana asks the other two to speak first
he says: you two speak first, I'll listen.
in the king's answer, all beings come out of space and go back into it
space is greater than all of them, the last support.

games.q: Pravahana says all beings come out of space and go back into it. the Brahma Sutra asks: what is that space?
o: just the empty air around us
Brahman, the one reality everything comes from
games.why: Brahman. only Brahman could be the source and end of all beings, so Vedanta's teachers read Pravahana's space as Brahman.

practice: At the end of each out-breath there's a small pause before the next breath comes; let your attention rest there without stretching it.
Then listen for the quiet between one sound and the next, and the gap after a passing thought, the open room everything else happens in. If you pray, rest in prayer there.

wordCard.voice: The Sama Veda as song. In the Chandogya, three singers ask what the chant rests on, all the way down to space, which Vedanta reads as Brahman. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: space, open room. In Chandogya 1.9 it is the last support of the high chant.

carryVoice: Your line: the last ground of everything is Brahman. The king called it space. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 1.8 (Shilaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana: the chant rests on tone, breath, food, water, the heavens, the earth)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.9.1–2 (all beings arise from space and return to it; space is the final support; the udgitha is without end)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.22 (ākāśas tal-liṅgāt: the 'space' of Chandogya 1.9.1 is Brahman), with Shankara's and Ramanuja's commentaries
